html:
The Chaná were an Indigenous people of the lower Paraná and Uruguay rivers, around the delta where they flow into the Río de la Plata, in what is now Argentina and Uruguay. (The chart item's name, Chané, belongs to a different people of the Chaco; the map's label here is Chaná.)

They lived on the islands and banks of the delta, fishing from canoes, hunting and gathering. Their language is related to that of the Charrúa. Spanish explorers met them from the 1520s, and over the next centuries they were absorbed into the colonial population.

Their language was long thought extinct. In the 2000s an elderly man in Entre Ríos, Blas Jaime, who had learned it from his family, worked with linguists to record it.
